sections.heading: Title
sections.text: Graph neural networks are fundamentally limited in what they can compute, and the standard yardstick for that power, the Weisfeiler-Lehman hierarchy, is both hard to interpret and too coarse to separate modern architectures. This ICML 2023 paper proposes a cleaner alternative: measure a graph network by which equivariant polynomials of the graph it can compute. The authors give a complete basis for these polynomials, where every basis element is simply a small multi-graph and evaluating it is a tensor contraction. They then build algorithmic tools to read off the exact polynomial power of popular models, and use the theory to design stronger networks that set state of the art on molecular graph benchmarks.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.text: The expressive power of graph neural networks, meaning which functions of a graph they can actually represent, is known to be bounded. The field measures this power with the Weisfeiler-Lehman hierarchy, a family of graph-isomorphism tests. But WL has two problems. Its definition is combinatorial and gives no recipe for making a network stronger, and its rungs are so far apart that many architecturally different GNNs collapse to the same WL level. The paper asks for a finer, more actionable measure of expressive power.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: The authors argue that the right way to grade a graph network is by the concrete quantities it can compute. Polynomials of the adjacency matrix that respect node relabeling, called equivariant graph polynomials, are natural candidates: subgraph counts and many structural features are exactly such polynomials. If we knew the full space of these polynomials and which ones a given network can evaluate, we would have both a fine-grained ruler and a to-do list of missing operations. Earlier results only described very low-degree cases, so a complete and practical characterization was needed.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: There are three contributions. First, a complete basis for all equivariant graph polynomials up to any degree, where each basis element corresponds to a directed multi-graph and computing it is a tensor contraction, an einsum. Second, algorithmic tools: the authors model a network as a bank of primitive contractions and give a linear-time algorithm that decides exactly which polynomials the network can compute, letting them tabulate the polynomial power of standard GNNs. Third, guided by this analysis they enhance existing models with precomputed polynomial features and extra operations, producing an improved provably powerful network they call PPGN++.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: The core object is a basis for equivariant graph polynomials. Each basis element is a directed multi-graph H with a marked red edge, and its value on a graph is a tensor contraction, an einsum expression that multiplies entries of the adjacency matrix according to the edges of H and sums over the internal nodes. To make these polynomials equivariant, monomials are averaged over all node permutations with the Reynolds operator, which the paper shows equals a sum over the orbit of H. To analyze a network, the authors treat it as a bank of primitive contractions and give a linear-time algorithm that decides whether a target polynomial can be assembled by repeatedly contracting nodes. Node-based banks turn out to equal 1-WL and edge-based banks equal 2-FWL, also known as 3-WL. Building on this, PPGN++ refines the powerful matrix-multiplication network with a small set of primitive operations and, crucially, feeds in precomputed polynomial features, which lifts it strictly above 3-WL.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.text: The experiments cover two settings. For real-world performance, the authors use three standard molecular regression datasets: ZINC with twelve thousand molecules, the larger ZINC-full with over two hundred thousand, and Alchemy, all measured by test mean absolute error, lower being better, and all models kept under a five-hundred-thousand parameter budget. For raw expressive power they use families of Strongly Regular graphs, which are notoriously hard to tell apart and cannot be separated by 3-WL, measuring the failure rate at distinguishing non-isomorphic pairs.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.text: The headline result is state of the art across the board. On ZINC-12K, PPGN++ with degree-six polynomial features reaches a test error of 0.071, beating strong baselines like CIN at 0.079 and GIN at 0.163. On ZINC-full it reaches 0.020, and on Alchemy 0.109, both best in class. Just as striking, the polynomial features are model-agnostic: bolting degree-six features onto a plain GatedGCN cuts its ZINC-12K error from 0.265 to 0.106. And because the features are precomputed, the network gains expressive power strictly beyond 3-WL without paying a heavy runtime cost.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.text: Two ablations tell the story. First, degree matters: on ZINC-12K, adding degree-five features gives 0.072 and degree-six gives 0.071, a steady improvement over the base 0.076, and the same trend appears on the other datasets. Second, on the Strongly Regular graphs, which 3-WL cannot separate at all, adding polynomial features drives the failure rate down by several orders of magnitude as the degree climbs from five to seven, for both GatedGCN and PPGN++. The theoretical counts in Table 1 back this up: the edge-based contraction bank can compute almost all low-degree polynomials, far more than the node-based bank.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.text: To fix the numbers in mind: on ZINC-12K, PPGN++ with degree-six features reaches 0.071 test error, the best reported. On ZINC-full it hits 0.020, and on Alchemy 0.109, both state of the art. Adding the same features to a GatedGCN backbone improves it from 0.265 to 0.106. All of this holds under a five-hundred-thousand parameter budget, and the resulting models are provably more expressive than the 3-WL test.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.text: The lasting message is that expressive power becomes concrete and constructive when you phrase it as: which equivariant graph polynomials can this network compute? Every such polynomial is just a small multi-graph evaluated by a tensor contraction, giving a finer ruler than Weisfeiler-Lehman and a direct list of missing operations. Acting on that list, precomputed polynomial features push ordinary graph networks past the 3-WL barrier and to the best accuracy on molecular property prediction, all within a modest parameter budget.
